pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew 'Amaryah, the LORD hath said)
etymology: Hebrew 'amar, to say, with Yah, the covenant name — the LORD hath said, or the LORD hath promised. Several men in Scripture bear it, most of them in the priestly line.
biblical_def: Amariah means the LORD hath said, and the men who bore it stand mostly in the high-priestly succession. The Chronicler places one between Meraioth and Ahitub: “Meraioth begat Amariah, and Amariah begat Ahitub” (1Ch 6:7), and another after Azariah: “And Azariah begat Amariah, and Amariah begat Ahitub” (1Ch 6:11). Ezra's own pedigree runs through the name: “The son of Amariah, the son of Azariah, the son of Meraioth” (Ezr 7:3). A Levite of Hebron's house bears it too: “Of the sons of Hebron; Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth” (1Ch 23:19). The most consequential Amariah is Jehoshaphat's chief priest, appointed over the ecclesiastical half of a divided jurisdiction: “And, behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, for all the king's matters” (2Ch 19:11). And the name reaches the prophets: Zephaniah is the son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah (Zep 1:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat proper names of Scripture; the sense is given by the Hebrew, from 'amar, to say, and Yah, the LORD — the LORD hath said or promised.
webster_full: AMARIAH. A Hebrew proper name; from amar, to say or promise, and Yah, the covenant name of God: the LORD hath said.
SAY, v.t. To speak; to utter in words; to declare.
PROMISE, n. In a general sense, a declaration, written or verbal, which binds the person who makes it, either in honor, conscience or law, to do or forbear a certain act.

corruption_summary: Genealogies are dismissed as filler to be skipped, when the priestly lists are the documentary spine that makes a claim like Ezra's testable.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the evidentiary function of the registers. Ezra 7 does not assert that Ezra was a priest; it traces him, name by name, back through Amariah and Azariah and Meraioth to Aaron the chief priest. A man who could not produce the line was put from the priesthood as polluted, and Nehemiah 7 records it happening. The lists are the mechanism by which the office stayed accountable.

2 Chronicles 19:11 deserves separate notice for what it establishes about jurisdiction. Jehoshaphat placed Amariah the chief priest over all matters of the LORD and Zebadiah over all the king's matters. That is a real distinction of spheres inside one covenant nation — neither the modern secularist wall that silences the church in public, nor the fusion that makes the magistrate a bishop. The Reformers' two-kingdoms doctrine has an Old Testament precedent, and this verse is it.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Bani, built, or the LORD hath built)
etymology: Hebrew banah, to build. The name is a shortened form of a longer confession — the LORD hath built — and the men who carried it appear at two moments of literal rebuilding.
biblical_def: Bani means built, and the name recurs from David's wars to the return from exile. One of David's mighty men bore it: “Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite” (2Sa 23:36). It stands in a Levitical line, “The son of Amzi, the son of Bani, the son of Shamer” (1Ch 6:46), and in the register of Judah's returned settlers, “the son of Bani, of the children of Pharez the son of Judah” (1Ch 9:4). A whole clan came back from Babylon under it: “The children of Bani, six hundred forty and two” (Ezr 2:10) — and some of those sons appear in Ezra's painful list of men who had taken foreign wives (Ezr 10:29). Two later moments matter most. When Ezra read the law from the wooden pulpit, Bani is named among the Levites who “caused the people to understand the law” (Neh 8:7); and at the great confession, “Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God” (Neh 9:4).

2. To raise by art; to frame or shape into a particular form.
3. In Scripture, to increase and strengthen; to cement and knit together; to settle or establish and preserve.

corruption_summary: Teaching is imagined as performance from a platform, while Nehemiah 8 describes Levites moving among the people until they understood the law.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in Nehemiah 8:7, where Bani and his fellow Levites caused the people to understand the law. Ezra read from the pulpit; the Levites made it land. The next verse says they gave the sense and caused them to understand the reading. That is exposition, and it is presented as a distinct labour from the public reading — the text was not assumed to explain itself, and the explaining was done by many men among the congregation rather than one man above it.

The name itself carries the theme. Bani means built, and the men who bore it appear in the two generations that had to rebuild — the returned exiles who came up with Zerubbabel and the Levites who stood on the stairs and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD. Psalm 127 supplies the caution over all of it: except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Ye'i'el, God sweeps away, or treasured of God)
etymology: A Hebrew name compounded with 'El, God. Borne by musicians, scribes, and Levites across four centuries of Israel's worship and administration.
biblical_def: Jeiel belongs mostly to the men who kept Israel's worship and its records. A Reubenite chief bore it (1Ch 5:7). Two appear among the musicians David set before the ark: “And Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps on the Sheminith to excel” (1Ch 15:21), and in the roster of the ministry, “Asaph the chief, and next to him Zechariah, Jeiel, and Shemiramoth… and Jeiel with psalteries and with harps” (1Ch 16:5). One kept the muster rolls for king Uzziah: “Moreover Uzziah had an host of fighting men, that went out to war by bands, according to the number of their account by the hand of Jeiel the scribe” (2Ch 26:11). One was among the Levites who cleansed the temple under Hezekiah (2Ch 29:13). And one gave lavishly for Josiah's passover: “Conaniah also, and Shemaiah and Nethaneel, his brethren, and Hashabiah and Jeiel and Jozabad, chief of the Levites, gave unto the Levites for passover offerings five thousand small cattle, and five hundred oxen” (2Ch 35:9). A Jeiel is also grandfather to Jahaziel, upon whom the Spirit of the LORD came in the congregation (2Ch 20:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, a compound ending in 'El, God, borne by Levites, musicians and scribes.
webster_full: JEIEL. A Hebrew proper name compounded with El, God.
SCRIBE, n. In Scripture and the Jewish history, a clerk or secretary to the king; also, a writer and a doctor of the law.
PSALTERY, n. An instrument of music used by the Hebrews, the form of which is not now known.

corruption_summary: Church music is treated as a matter of taste and atmosphere, while the Chronicler records it as an appointed office with named men, assigned instruments and specified duty.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Israel's music was an ordinance, not an ambience. The Chronicler names the players, assigns the instruments — Jeiel with psalteries and with harps, Asaph with cymbals — and specifies the setting, harps on the Sheminith. David set them there by command, and 2 Chronicles 29:25 says the commandment was of the LORD by his prophets. The regulative principle governs the music as much as the sacrifice.

The second Jeiel worth pausing over is the scribe who numbered Uzziah's army. The same chapter ends with Uzziah strong, and lifted up to his destruction, going into the temple to burn incense and struck with leprosy at the altar. The registers Jeiel kept were the record of a strength that became the king's snare. Chronicles is careful about both facts and never lets the second cancel the first.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Yo'ach, the LORD is brother)
etymology: Hebrew Yah, the covenant name, with 'ach, brother — the LORD is brother. The most prominent bearer stood on Jerusalem's wall the day Rabshakeh came.
biblical_def: The best-known Joah is Hezekiah's recorder, one of three officials sent out to the Assyrian field commander. “And when they had called to the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder” (2Ki 18:18). The three made a request that Rabshakeh contemptuously refused: “Then said Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and Shebna, and Joah, unto Rabshakeh, Speak, I pray thee, to thy servants in the Syrian language; for we understand it: and talk not with us in the Jews' language in the ears of the people that are on the wall” (2Ki 18:26). They had been ordered to say nothing, and they obeyed; and when it was over, “Then came Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder, to Hezekiah with their clothes rent, and told him the words of Rabshakeh” (2Ki 18:37). Other men bear the name: a Levite in the line of Gershom (1Ch 6:21), and the third son of Obededom among the porters (1Ch 26:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, from Yah, the LORD, and 'ach, brother — the LORD is brother.
webster_full: JOAH. A Hebrew proper name; from Yah, the LORD, and ach, brother: the LORD is brother.
RECORDER, n. One whose official duty is to register writings or transactions; an officer who keeps the rolls.
2. In Scripture, an officer of high rank in the court of the kings of Judah, keeping the annals of the kingdom.
scriptures: And when they had called to the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder.

Moreover the sons of Obededom were, Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, and Sacar the fourth, and Nethaneel the fifth,
corruption_summary: Silence before mockery is read as weakness, while Hezekiah's officers held their peace under orders and carried the blasphemy to the one who could answer it.
corruption_paragraphs: Joah's hour was one of the most public humiliations in Israel's history, and his conduct in it is instructive. Rabshakeh stood before the wall and blasphemed the LORD in the Jews' language so that every man on the ramparts would hear. The king had commanded, Answer him not. So three officers stood there, said nothing, and then rent their clothes and carried the words to Hezekiah — who took them into the house of the LORD and spread them before Him. Restraint here was not cowardice; it was the refusal to fight on the enemy's chosen ground.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the office itself. A recorder kept the annals of the kingdom, which means Judah maintained a written record of what happened, including what happened badly. The Chronicler's and the Kings historian's willingness to preserve national disgrace — the tribute stripped from the temple doors two verses earlier — is the mark of a record kept before God rather than for a king's reputation.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Zebadyah, the LORD hath given)
etymology: Hebrew zabad, to bestow or endow, with Yah — the LORD hath given. The same verb Leah used when she said God had endued her with a good dowry.
biblical_def: Zebadiah means the LORD hath given, and nine or more men in Scripture bear it, spread across Benjamin, the porters, the army and the priesthood. Two stand in the Benjamite registers (1Ch 8:15, 8:17). Two of Jeroham's sons of Gedor joined David at Ziklag: “And Joelah, and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor” (1Ch 12:7). One was third son among the porters: “And the sons of Meshelemiah were, Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth” (1Ch 26:2). One commanded a monthly course of twenty-four thousand men: “The fourth captain for the fourth month was Asahel the brother of Joab, and Zebadiah his son after him” (1Ch 27:7). One was among the Levites Jehoshaphat sent through Judah with the book of the law (2Ch 17:8). And one held the civil half of Jehoshaphat's judiciary: “Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, for all the king's matters” (2Ch 19:11).

corruption_summary: Civil office is imagined as a secular sphere untouched by God's claim, while Jehoshaphat set a Zebadiah over the king's matters under the same charge to deal courageously in the fear of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Chronicles 19 is the fullest description of a judiciary in the Old Testament, and it does not divide the world into sacred and secular. Amariah the chief priest is over all matters of the LORD; Zebadiah the ruler of the house of Judah is over all the king's matters. Two jurisdictions, distinct offices, and one charge covering both: Deal courageously, and the LORD shall be with the good. The spheres are real; the Lordship over them is undivided.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in 2 Chronicles 17:8, where Jehoshaphat sent Zebadiah and other Levites through the cities of Judah with the book of the law in their hand. A reformation begun by circuit teaching, not by decree. The king had the power to command conformity and instead spent it on getting the text into the hands of men who could explain it, which is the pattern every genuine reform in Judah followed.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew 'Adayah, the LORD hath adorned, or whom the LORD adorns)
etymology: Hebrew 'adah, to pass on, to deck or adorn, with Yah — adorned of the LORD. One bearer is the grandfather of king Josiah.
biblical_def: Adaiah stands in several registers, and one bearer sits at the head of Judah's last great reformation. The record of Josiah's reign opens with him: “Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty and one years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath” (2Ki 22:1). Josiah's father Amon was murdered after two wicked years; his mother Jedidah, whose name means beloved, was the daughter of this otherwise unknown man of Boscath. Others bear the name: a Levite in the line of Gershom (1Ch 6:41), a Benjamite (1Ch 8:21), a priest of the returned remnant, “And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah” (1Ch 9:12), and the father of one of the captains Jehoiada took into covenant when he overthrew Athaliah: “and Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri” (2Ch 23:1). Two of Ezra's lists of men who put away foreign wives contain the name as well (Ezr 10:29, 10:39).

corruption_summary: Godly influence is measured by visible platform, while the man who shaped Judah's last reformation is named once, as somebody's grandfather from an obscure town.
corruption_paragraphs: Adaiah of Boscath appears in Scripture in a single clause, and Boscath is a town in the lowland of Judah mentioned twice in the whole Bible. His daughter Jedidah raised the boy who became king at eight, who at sixteen began to seek after the God of David, and who at twenty-six purged the land and kept the greatest passover since the days of the judges. Nothing is recorded of Adaiah's piety. Only the line: 2 Kings troubles itself to say whose daughter Josiah's mother was.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture keeps these names on purpose. The historian who tells us the name of Josiah's maternal grandfather and the village he came from is telling us that reformations are not spontaneous, that a boy king with a godly mother is not an accident, and that God is at work in households nobody is watching. Most of the men who mattered most in redemptive history are named once.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew 'Eli'el, my God is God)
etymology: Hebrew 'eli, my God, doubled with 'El, God — a name that is itself a confession: my God is God. Nine or more men bear it.
biblical_def: Eliel means my God is God, and the men who bore it are soldiers, Levites and overseers. Among the half-tribe of Manasseh east of Jordan: “And these were the heads of the house of their fathers, even Epher, and Ishi, and Eliel, and Azriel, and Jeremiah, and Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of the house of their fathers” (1Ch 5:24). One stands in Samuel's own Levitical line, “The son of Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Eliel, the son of Toah” (1Ch 6:34). Two are named among the Benjamites of Jerusalem (1Ch 8:20, 8:22). One is a mighty man of David's: “Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam” (1Ch 11:46), and another among the Gadites who came to David at the hold, “Attai the sixth, Eliel the seventh” (1Ch 12:11). And one served in Hezekiah's reform as a treasury overseer: “And Jehiel, and Azaziah, and Nahath, and Asahel, and Jerimoth, and Jozabad, and Eliel… were overseers under the hand of Cononiah” (2Ch 31:13).

The son of Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Eliel, the son of Toah,
Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite,

And Jehiel, and Azaziah, and Nahath, and Asahel, and Jerimoth, and Jozabad, and Eliel, and Ismachiah, and Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers under the hand of Cononiah and Shimei his brother, at the commandment of Hezekiah the king, and Azariah the ruler of the house of God.
corruption_summary: God is spoken of as a personal preference, while a name borne by nine ordinary Israelites insists that the God who is mine is God absolutely.
corruption_paragraphs: The name is a whole theology in two words. My God is God — the possessive and the absolute in one breath. Modern religious speech is fluent in the first half and embarrassed by the second: people will readily say what God means to them and hesitate to say what God is. Eliel refuses the split. The God who is mine is not mine because I have chosen Him; He is mine because He is God, and my claiming Him adds nothing to His being.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Israelite parents put confessions in their children's mouths. A boy named Eliel could not introduce himself without stating a doctrine. The practice assumes what our age doubts — that faith is transmitted deliberately, through households, in the ordinary furniture of a life, and that a child is formed by what he is given to say long before he can weigh it.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Eli'el (H447), my God is God; from 'el (H410), God, with the first-person suffix; the same element in Elijah, Elisha, Eliezer, Elkanah.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Eli'el (H447) — Eliel; 1 Chronicles 5:24, 6:34, 11:46, 2 Chronicles 31:13.
Hebrew 'El (H410) — God, the Mighty One; both elements of the name.
Hebrew gibbor chayil — mighty men of valour; the description in 1 Chronicles 5:24.
Hebrew paqid (H6496) — overseer; Eliel's office under Hezekiah.
Hebrew 'Eliyahu (H452) — Elijah, my God is the LORD; the same construction.
usage: “Mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of the house of their fathers” — the company Eliel kept.
“Eliel the Mahavite” — among David's mighty men.
The name is a sentence: my God is God.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Zikri, memorable, or my remembrance)
etymology: Hebrew zakar, to remember — the root of zikkaron, memorial, and of the recorder's title. The name means remembered, and one bearer is remembered for a very dark deed.
biblical_def: Zichri means memorable, and a dozen men carry it. The first is a Levite of the highest rank and worst family: “And the sons of Izhar; Korah, and Nepheg, and Zichri” (Exo 6:21) — brother to the Korah who perished in his rebellion. Several stand in the Benjamite lists of Jerusalem (1Ch 8:19, 8:23, 8:27), and one in the line of Asaph: “And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph” (1Ch 9:15). One is the father of a captain who helped Jehoiada overthrow Athaliah (2Ch 23:1). But the Zichri Scripture recalls most sharply belongs to the reign of Ahaz, when Judah was given into the hand of Israel: “And Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, slew Maaseiah the king's son, and Azrikam the governor of the house, and Elkanah that was next to the king” (2Ch 28:7). Three men in one verse, the king's son among them, killed by an Israelite in a war between brothers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, from zakar, to remember — memorable, or my remembrance.
webster_full: ZICHRI. A Hebrew proper name; from zakar, to remember: memorable.
REMEMBER, v.t. To have in the mind an idea which had been in the mind before, and which recurs to the mind without effort.
MEMORIAL, n. That which preserves the memory of something; any thing that serves to keep in memory.
scriptures: Exo 6:21
And the sons of Izhar; Korah, and Nepheg, and Zichri.
And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph;

And in the seventh year Jehoiada strengthened himself, and took the captains of hundreds, Azariah the son of Jeroham, and Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, and Azariah the son of Obed, and Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri, into covenant with him.
And Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, slew Maaseiah the king's son, and Azrikam the governor of the house, and Elkanah that was next to the king.
corruption_summary: Civil war among the covenant people is treated as ordinary politics, while 2 Chronicles 28 records Israelites killing Judahites and a prophet stopping the army at the gate.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Chronicles 28 is one of the most disturbing chapters in the historical books, and the Zichri of verse 7 stands at the centre of it. Ahaz had led Judah into idolatry, and the LORD gave him into the hand of Pekah king of Israel, whose army slew a hundred and twenty thousand in one day. Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, killed the king's son and two of the highest officers of the realm. These were not foreign invaders. Ephraim and Judah were brothers, and the sword between them was raised by the LORD's own judgment on Ahaz.

The chapter does not end there, and the ending is what makes it Scripture rather than atrocity. The prophet Oded met the returning army and told them their own sins stood before God, and four named men of Ephraim rose up against those that came from the war, clothed the captives, fed them, and carried the feeble on asses to Jericho. The name Zichri means remembered. So are the four who turned the army around, and Scripture records both kinds of memory in the same chapter.
roots_summary: Hebrew Zikri (H2147), memorable; from zakar (H2142), to remember; cognate with zikkaron (H2146), memorial, and mazkir, the recorder.
roots_lines: Hebrew Zikri (H2147) — Zichri; Exodus 6:21, 1 Chronicles 9:15, 2 Chronicles 28:7.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember; the root of the name.
Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — memorial; the stones on the priest's shoulders.
Hebrew Yitshar (H3324) — Izhar; father of Korah, Nepheg and Zichri.
Hebrew gibbor (H1368) — mighty man; the description of the Zichri of 2 Chronicles 28:7.
usage: “The sons of Izhar; Korah, and Nepheg, and Zichri” — brother to the rebel.
“Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, slew Maaseiah the king's son” — brother against brother.
The name means remembered. Scripture remembers both what he did and who undid it.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew Beri'ah, in trouble, or a gift)
etymology: The Chronicler supplies the etymology himself: Ephraim called his son Beriah because it went evil with his house, connecting the name with Hebrew ra'ah, evil or calamity.
biblical_def: Beriah is a name given out of grief and preserved as a tribe. The first bearer is a son of Asher: “And the sons of Asher; Jimnah, and Ishuah, and Isui, and Beriah, and Serah their sister: and the sons of Beriah; Heber, and Malchiel” (Gen 46:17). His descendants became a clan counted in the wilderness census: “Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the family of the Heberites: of Malchiel, the family of the Malchielites” (Num 26:45). The second bearer is the one whose naming Scripture explains. Ephraim's sons had been killed by the men of Gath, and the patriarch mourned many days; then: “And when he went in to his wife, she conceived, and bare a son, and he called his name Beriah, because it went evil with his house” (1Ch 7:23). A child born into a house still in mourning was named for the calamity that made room for him. Other Beriahs stand among the Benjamites (1Ch 8:13) and the Levites of David's courses (1Ch 23:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the Chronicler gives the sense, from the Hebrew for evil or calamity — because it went evil with his house.
webster_full: BERIAH. A Hebrew proper name; explained in 1 Chronicles 7:23 from the word for evil or misfortune.
CALAMITY, n. Any great misfortune, or cause of misery; generally applied to events or disasters which produce extensive evils.
MOURN, v.i. To grieve; to lament; to sorrow; to be sorrowful.
scriptures: And the sons of Asher; Jimnah, and Ishuah, and Isui, and Beriah, and Serah their sister: and the sons of Beriah; Heber, and Malchiel.
Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the family of the Heberites: of Malchiel, the family of the Malchielites.
And when he went in to his wife, she conceived, and bare a son, and he called his name Beriah, because it went evil with his house.
And the sons of Beriah; Heber, and Malchiel, who is the father of Birzavith.
corruption_summary: Grief is expected to be resolved before life resumes, while Scripture records a father naming a son for the sorrow he was born into and the line continuing anyway.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Chronicles 7:23 is one of the quietest and hardest verses in the genealogies. Ephraim's sons were slain, he mourned many days, his brethren came to comfort him — and then he went in to his wife and she bare a son, and he named the boy for the disaster. The modern instinct would counsel against it: do not lay that on a child. Scripture does not comment. It reports the naming and moves on, and the line of Beriah runs forward into the tribe.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture allows grief to be named without requiring it to be resolved. Naomi called herself Mara and the book did not correct her. Ephraim called his son Beriah. Neither is presented as a model of faith or a failure of it; both are recorded, and in both cases God's purpose ran through the house that mourned. A daughter of this same Beriah, Sherah, went on to build three cities.
roots_summary: Hebrew Beri'ah (H1283); the Chronicler links it to ra'ah (H7451), evil or calamity, in the phrase because it went evil with his house.
roots_lines: Hebrew Beri'ah (H1283) — Beriah; Genesis 46:17, 1 Chronicles 7:23, 8:13.
Hebrew ra'ah (H7451) — evil, calamity; the word the Chronicler uses to explain the name.
Hebrew 'abal (H56) — to mourn; Ephraim mourned many days.
Hebrew mishpachah (H4940) — family, clan; the Beriites of Numbers 26:44.
Hebrew 'Asher (H836) — Asher, happy; the tribe of the first Beriah, whose own name means blessed.
usage: “He called his name Beriah, because it went evil with his house” — the sorrow written into the child.
“The family of the Beriites” — a clan out of a grief.
The Chronicler explains the name and offers no consolation. The line continues.

pos: n. pr. m. (Hebrew 'Abishua', father of welfare, or my father is deliverance)
etymology: Hebrew 'ab, father, with a root of prosperity or salvation — father of welfare. The chief bearer is the fourth high priest of Israel, great-grandson of Aaron.
biblical_def: Abishua stands in the shortest and most consequential stretch of genealogy in the Old Testament: the descent of the high priesthood from Aaron. “Eleazar begat Phinehas, Phinehas begat Abishua” (1Ch 6:4), and the line runs on, “And Abishua begat Bukki, and Bukki begat Uzzi” (1Ch 6:5). The Chronicler repeats it in the roll of Aaron's sons: “And these are the sons of Aaron; Eleazar his son, Phinehas his son, Abishua his son” (1Ch 6:50). And Ezra's own genealogy, offered to establish his right to act, runs back through him to the beginning: “The son of Abishua, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the chief priest” (Ezr 7:5). A different Abishua is listed among the Benjamites, a son of Bela (1Ch 8:4). Nothing else is recorded of the priest — no act, no word, no length of service. He is a link, and the chain he is in is the reason we know it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, from 'ab, father, with a root of welfare or salvation — father of prosperity.
webster_full: ABISHUA. A Hebrew proper name; from ab, father, with a root signifying welfare or deliverance.
PRIEST, n. A man who officiates in sacred offices; one who presents to God the offerings of the people.
SUCCESSION, n. A following of things in order; a series of persons or things following each other in time or place.
scriptures: Eleazar begat Phinehas, Phinehas begat Abishua,
And Abishua begat Bukki, and Bukki begat Uzzi,
And these are the sons of Aaron; Eleazar his son, Phinehas his son, Abishua his son,
Ezr 7:5
The son of Abishua, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the chief priest:
corruption_summary: A priesthood proved by descent is treated as tribal accident, while Hebrews argues from that very succession that Christ's priesthood is of a different and better order.
corruption_paragraphs: The Aaronic line exists in Scripture partly to be superseded. Hebrews takes up exactly these genealogies and argues that the Levitical priests were made without an oath, that they were many because death would not let them continue, and that Christ is a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec — without father, without mother, without descent. Abishua's whole recorded significance is that he was somebody's son and somebody's father, and that is precisely the argument: this priesthood was a chain of mortal men, and one of them was always burying another.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the New Testament reasons from the Old Testament's documentary detail rather than around it. Hebrews 7 does not spiritualize the genealogy; it reads it, notices what it says and what it omits, and builds a doctrine on both. Readers who skip the lists are skipping the premises of an apostolic argument.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Abishua' (H50), father of welfare; from 'ab (H1), father, and a root of prosperity or salvation; the line is kohen gadol, high priest.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Abishua' (H50) — Abishua; 1 Chronicles 6:4, 6:50, Ezra 7:5.
Hebrew 'ab (H1) — father; the first element of the name.
Hebrew Pinechas (H6372) — Phinehas, his father, of the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.
Hebrew kohen gadol — high priest; the office the line carried.
Greek Melchisedek (G3198) — Melchisedec; the order Hebrews sets against this succession.
usage: “Phinehas begat Abishua” — four generations from Aaron.
“The son of Abishua, the son of Phinehas… the son of Aaron the chief priest” — Ezra's warrant.
Nothing is recorded of him but his place in the chain, and the chain is the point.
